In LLM inference, what does “KV” in “KV cache” stand for?
a) Key-Value
b) Kernel-Vector
c) Knowledge-Vault
✅ Answer: a) Key-Value. These are the attention keys and values a model computes for each token.
Tensormesh’s founders created which open-source project for storing and reusing KV cache?
a) LangChain
b) LMCache
c) llama.cpp
✅ Answer: b) LMCache. It’s used with inference engines like vLLM.
3. What’s the main benefit of using the Tensormesh platform for KV cache?
a) It makes your model bigger
b) It improves your training data
c) It reuses work the model has already done, so you get faster responses and lower inference costs on fewer GPUs
✅ Answer: c). Tensormesh stores the KV cache and reuses it across requests, so GPUs don’t recompute tokens they’ve already processed.

All Answers A are the correct answers:

1. Why is it hard to spot an AI agent in a Kubernetes cluster?
A. To Kubernetes, an AI agent looks like any other pod 
B. AI agents run outside the cluster
C. AI agents don’t get IP addresses
D. Kubernetes hides AI agents by default
Why: Nothing in the pod spec says “this is an AI agent.” You have to look at what it does.

2. Why are shared API keys a problem for AI agents?
A. You can’t tell which AI agent used the key, and revoking it breaks everyone who shares it 
B. They make LLM calls slower
C. Kubernetes can’t store them
D. They expire every minute
Why: Each AI agent needs its own identity, not a shared secret.

3. You delete a misbehaving AI agent’s pod. What usually happens next?
A. Its Deployment recreates the pod 
B. The AI agent is gone for good
C. The whole namespace is deleted
D. The node reboots
Why: Kubernetes keeps restoring the state you declared, so deleting a pod rarely stops anything.
